questions.stem: The board pack for your library refurbishment programme is circulated at half past eight for a nine o'clock meeting, because you wait for the last cost figures to land. The chair spends the first twenty minutes reading sections aloud, and the two decisions on the agenda have now been deferred for a fourth month. Your sponsor asks you to make the meeting shorter. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Issue the pack three working days ahead using the previous Friday's figures, marking anything still provisional.
options.rationale: Reading has to happen before the meeting for the meeting to be about deciding. Slightly older figures with the provisional parts flagged cost less than another month of deferral.

options.text: Keep the timing and cut the pack to two pages so it can be read in the room.
options.rationale: It treats length as the fault when the fault is that reading is consuming decision time. A shorter pack read at the table still leaves nobody prepared to weigh anything.

options.text: Walk the group through the pack as slides at the start of each meeting.
options.rationale: This formalises reading in the room rather than removing it, and a presented pack is harder to interrogate than one people have already annotated.

options.text: Ask the chair to defer both decisions to a special meeting once members have read the pack.
options.rationale: It moves the cost rather than removing it, adds a meeting to a group already short of time, and delays two decisions that are three months late.

questions.explanation: A decision forum can only decide if the reading has already happened, so the publication lead time is set by how long the audience needs, not by when the last number arrives. Where those conflict, a figure that is a few days old and labelled as such is nearly always worth more than a fresh one nobody has absorbed. Timeliness in reporting means in time to be used, not as late as possible.
questions.mindset: Send information early enough to be read, because unread information has not been communicated.

questions.stem: Your squad builds scheduling software for a community energy co-operative. After every sprint review the recording and a short summary go into the team's chat workspace. The two directors who release the funding are not members of that workspace and have seen nothing for six weeks. At yesterday's board one of them asked whether the team had started work yet. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the two directors how and how often they want updates, and then send them that way.
options.rationale: Delivery is defined at the receiving end. Asking takes a minute and replaces a guess about their habits with the arrangement they will actually use.

options.text: Add them to the chat workspace and show them where to find the channel.
options.rationale: It assumes the barrier is access when the barrier is that they do not work in that tool. The cost of adopting your channel is placed on the busiest people in the audience.

options.text: Post the recordings more often and add a written summary to the channel.
options.rationale: Increasing volume in a channel the audience does not read changes nothing for them, and it uses effort that would have been better spent asking one question.

options.text: Ask the directors' assistants to pass the updates on.
options.rationale: A relay strips out the detail that made the update worth sending, and it leaves you with no way of knowing whether anything reached the people who fund the work.

questions.explanation: A channel only exists where the audience already reads. Publishing somewhere convenient for the sender and calling that communication is the most common way an informed team ends up with an uninformed sponsor. When an audience has gone quiet, the first question is not what to send them but where they read, and the cheapest way to find that out is to ask them.
questions.mindset: Choose the channel the audience already reads, not the one that is easiest to publish to.

questions.stem: You manage a furnace upgrade at a glass recycling plant. Walking out to the car park, the operations director tells you to move the shutdown from May to June so the plant can protect its quarter. Nothing is written down. Twice already this quarter a corridor instruction has later been described as thinking aloud, after your planning had moved and a contractor had been rebooked. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send her a short note the same day recording what you took the instruction to be, what you will change, and by when a correction must reach you.
options.rationale: It keeps the speed of the informal channel and adds the record the channel lacks. The correction deadline turns her silence into a decision rather than leaving it ambiguous.

options.text: Stop acting on anything said outside a formal meeting until it is confirmed in writing.
options.rationale: It punishes a stakeholder for an informal style and slows down decisions that are perfectly real. The gap is the record, not the corridor.

options.text: Raise the pattern at the next steering group as a governance failure.
options.rationale: It escalates a fixable habit into a complaint about a senior colleague, spends credibility on it, and still leaves the note you have not written unwritten.

options.text: Ask her to put future instructions in writing herself.
options.rationale: It assigns the effort to the person with the least incentive to make the record. The person who needs the decision to hold is the one who should capture it.

questions.explanation: Verbal decisions are legitimate and often necessary; unrecorded ones are the problem, and the cure is a confirming note rather than a rule against talking. Written back promptly, with what will change and a date for objection, the note converts a recollection into something both parties have had the chance to correct. Whoever depends on the decision holding is the person who should carry the cost of recording it.
questions.mindset: The person who needs a decision to hold is the person who should write it down.

questions.stem: The squad building the dispensing platform for an online opticians works across six tools: chat, email, a wiki, a ticket tracker, a shared whiteboard and video calls. Last week a developer implemented a prescription validation rule that had been corrected during a video call, in the call's chat pane, which nobody reopened. In the retrospective the team asks to consolidate everything into a single tool. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree which single place is authoritative for each kind of information — decisions, requirements and day-to-day chatter — and leave the tool set alone.
options.rationale: It fixes the fault, which is that no class of information has a known home. Naming the home for decisions costs nothing and survives whatever tools the team uses next year.

options.text: Move all project communication into the ticket tracker so everything is traceable.
options.rationale: Forcing low-value conversation into a heavyweight tool makes people route around it, and the traceability that motivated the move is the first thing lost.

options.text: Ask everyone to copy anything important into the wiki.
options.rationale: It relies on each person judging importance in the moment, doubles the work, and creates a second copy that starts diverging from the first immediately.

options.text: Rule that no decision may be taken during a video call.
options.rationale: It bans the medium that resolves disagreements fastest, when the failure was in what happened after the decision rather than where it was reached.

questions.explanation: Tool sprawl is rarely the real complaint. What hurts a team is having no agreed answer to where a particular class of information lives, so a decision can be reached in one place and looked for in another. Deciding the home for each class — what is durable, what is disposable, what must be findable in a year — is a cheap agreement that outlasts any tool, and it is the thing consolidation is usually a proxy for.
questions.mindset: Decide where each kind of information lives before deciding which tools to use.

questions.stem: Your programme is replacing the appointment system used by a national blood donation service. The fortnightly progress report goes out as a scanned document with the status table embedded as a picture. A senior clinician on the assurance group, who uses a screen reader, has twice asked a colleague to read it to her. She has now stopped commenting on the reports altogether. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reissue the report in a structured format with the status expressed as text, and check with her that the new version works.
options.rationale: It repairs the artefact everyone receives rather than the experience of one reader, and checking closes the loop instead of assuming the fix landed.

options.text: Telephone her before each report to talk her through it.
options.rationale: A workaround makes her dependent on your diary for information everyone else gets independently, and the report stays unreadable for anyone else in the same position.

options.text: Ask her to raise a formal accessibility request so the change is properly authorised.
options.rationale: It routes a fix you could make this afternoon through a process built for something else, and asks the person disadvantaged by the format to do the work of changing it.

options.text: Keep the format and add a plain-text summary at the top of the covering email.
options.rationale: It concedes that the report itself stays unreadable and leaves her with the summary while everyone else has the substance, which is what caused her to disengage.

questions.explanation: A communication that a member of the audience cannot read has not been sent to them, and the audience list is the test of whether a format is adequate. Building the artefact so everyone can use it is cheaper than maintaining parallel arrangements and it does not require anyone to identify themselves as needing help. Silence from a stakeholder who used to respond is usually a signal about the channel before it is a signal about the content.
questions.mindset: Build the artefact so that everyone in the audience can read it, rather than making one person ask.

questions.stem: Your restoration of a heritage railway's carriage works is funded by a grant with a public engagement condition. The communications plan promises a weekly bulletin to two hundred volunteers and a monthly funder update. You have missed three of the last five bulletins. Volunteers now say they learn things from the café rota sheet, and two have told a trustee that the project is being run secretively. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Move the bulletin to a cadence you can sustain, and say openly that you are doing so and why.
options.rationale: A smaller promise kept is worth more than a larger one missed, and announcing the change stops the new rhythm being read as a further lapse.

options.text: Agree what the bulletin exists to let volunteers do, and cut everything that does not serve it.
options.rationale: Defining the purpose is what makes a sustainable cadence possible, because most of the effort was going into content nobody needed.

options.text: Hand the bulletin to a volunteer coordinator so the weekly cadence is met.
options.rationale: It treats cadence as the goal and delegates a commitment without the information behind it, while you remain accountable for what it says.

options.text: Apologise for the gaps and catch up with a combined issue covering the missed weeks.
options.rationale: A catch-up issue restores volume rather than trust, and news from three weeks ago is not worth the reading time it asks for.

options.text: Stop the bulletin and rely on the café rota sheet, since that is where information already travels.
options.rationale: It accepts an unmanaged channel as the plan, so nothing you choose to say has a route, and the secrecy complaint gets louder rather than quieter.

questions.explanation: A communications plan is a set of promises to an audience, and its value comes from being kept rather than from being ambitious. When a cadence proves unsustainable, the repair is to reset the promise publicly and shrink the content to what the audience needs in order to act, not to catch up or to quietly stop. A missed update communicates something, and what it communicates is rarely what you would have written.
questions.mindset: Promise the cadence you can keep, because a missed update says more than the update would have.

questions.stem: After a billing outage on your electric vehicle charging network you set up a half-hour call at eight each morning across six teams. The outage was resolved seven weeks ago. Attendance has fallen from nineteen to six, the call routinely ends after four minutes, and two engineers have said they schedule their deep work around it. One area lead still uses it to flag site faults. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Close the call, and put in place a specific route for the one thing it is still being used for.
options.rationale: It ends a channel whose purpose has expired while preserving the remaining need, which is what stops the call being quietly restarted a month later.

options.text: Keep the call but reduce it to twice a week.
options.rationale: Halving a cost without asking whether the purpose survives leaves a meeting that outlives its reason more slowly, and it still fragments two engineers' mornings.

options.text: Make attendance mandatory again so the six who still come are not carrying it.
options.rationale: It reads falling attendance as indiscipline rather than as information about value, and compulsory presence produces bodies rather than attention.

options.text: Keep the slot in the diary in case a similar incident happens.
options.rationale: It holds a standing cost against a hypothetical event, when a call of this kind can be convened within the hour on the day it is actually needed.

questions.explanation: Every recurring communication should be created with a stated purpose and an end condition, because the effort of stopping one is always greater than the effort of starting it. Falling attendance and a four-minute agenda are the evidence that the purpose has been served; the discipline is to retire the channel and route whatever residual need remains somewhere proportionate. Communication load is a real cost carried by everyone except the person who scheduled it.
questions.mindset: Give every recurring meeting an end condition at the moment you create it.

questions.stem: Your district heating scheme cannot begin trenching until the environment regulator issues a permit, which has been with them for five weeks with no indication of a date. There is genuinely nothing new: no progress, no decision, no revised programme. You have skipped the last three fortnightly updates to the residents' liaison group. Two councillors have started asking officers whether the scheme has been cancelled. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Issue the update on schedule, saying what is being waited on, who holds it, and when you will next know something.
options.rationale: It keeps the promised rhythm and gives the audience the two facts they lack: where the project sits and when the picture changes next.

options.text: Wait until the permit arrives so that the next update carries something definite.
options.rationale: It treats an update as an announcement of progress, while the audience fills the gap with a worse story than the truth of a regulatory wait.

options.text: Send an update describing the preparatory work the team has done in the meantime.
options.rationale: Substituting activity for the question people are actually asking reads as evasion the moment somebody notices the permit is still not mentioned.

options.text: Ask the councillors' officers to reassure them that the scheme is still live.
options.rationale: It uses a relay to correct a rumour your own silence created, and the liaison group you actually committed to is still hearing nothing.

questions.explanation: Silence is a message whose content the audience supplies, and the story they invent is usually worse than the one you were reluctant to send. A cycle where the honest content is that nothing has moved is still worth issuing, because it confirms the project is being watched and tells people when to look again. Cadence is a commitment about when you will speak, not about having something impressive to say.
questions.mindset: Report on the promised cadence even when the news is that nothing has changed.

questions.stem: A cold storage operator's warehouse control project holds a weekly coordination meeting of ninety minutes with fourteen attendees. Reviewing four weeks of notes, you find that only three people ever speak, and that everything covered also appears in the written report issued the following morning. Before proposing a change, work out what the meeting consumes and be clear about which method the written report is.

blanks.label: Attendee time consumed by one meeting, in hours
blanks.rationale: Fourteen people for one and a half hours is 21 attendee-hours. The cost of a meeting is the whole room's time, not the ninety minutes the organiser books.

blanks.label: Attendee time consumed across a 48-week year, in hours
blanks.rationale: 21 hours a week over 48 weeks is 1,008 attendee-hours, or most of a person-year. Recurring costs are invisible per instance and material in aggregate.

blanks.label: The category of communication method a report issued afterwards belongs to
blanks.rationale: A report sent to a distribution list is push: it is directed at recipients whether or not they engage. Interactive methods, which cost attendee time, are justified only where the exchange itself is needed.

questions.explanation: Choosing a communication method is a cost decision as much as an effectiveness one, and the cost of an interactive method is everyone's time rather than the sender's. Interaction earns its price where something has to be negotiated, decided or understood together; where information is simply being conveyed, and is also going out in writing, the room is being paid for twice. Counting the aggregate hours is what makes a recurring cost visible enough to challenge.
questions.mindset: Count what a meeting costs in other people's hours before deciding it is cheap.

questions.stem: On a kiln control upgrade at a cement works, the supplier's project manager copies your sponsor into every message, including routine queries about cable routes. Your sponsor has begun answering some of them directly and has twice given the supplier an answer that contradicts what your engineers had agreed the previous week. The supplier now treats those answers as instructions. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with the supplier and the sponsor which matters go to whom, and move routine traffic onto a route that does not include the sponsor.
options.rationale: It addresses both halves of the problem — what the supplier sends and what the sponsor answers — and it does so by design rather than by asking people to show restraint.

options.text: Ask the supplier to stop copying your sponsor into routine correspondence.
options.rationale: It fixes only the sending half. A sponsor willing to answer whatever reaches him will keep being asked, through some other route, by someone who wants a faster answer.

options.text: Ask your sponsor not to reply to messages from the supplier.
options.rationale: It asks a senior stakeholder to ignore correspondence addressed to him, which is neither realistic nor his fault, and it leaves him uninformed about what he should be seeing.

options.text: Copy yourself into everything and correct the record whenever the sponsor answers wrongly.
options.rationale: It makes you a full-time corrector of an avoidable problem, and every correction confirms to the supplier that the sponsor is a usable channel worth trying again.

questions.explanation: Who hears what is a design decision, and where the project manager does not make it the loudest or most senior available channel makes it instead. Routine traffic, escalation and decision-making need separate routes with the sponsor's involvement defined rather than assumed, because a senior person answering a question they lack context for is a predictable consequence of receiving it. Fixing routing means changing what arrives, not asking people to be disciplined about what they do with it.
questions.mindset: Design who hears what, or the loudest available channel will decide it for you.

questions.stem: You run a school building programme for a local authority. Your monthly commentary describes an eight-week structural delay as some pressure on the programme timeline. The assurance lead has explained that these reports are disclosable on request and that plainer wording could end up quoted in the local paper. Your sponsor read last month's commentary as routine and did not release the contingency you had asked for. What should the project manager do?

options.text: State the delay, its cause and the decision you need in plain terms, and manage the disclosure risk through accuracy rather than vagueness.
options.rationale: An accurate account survives being quoted far better than a vague one does, and it is the only version that gets the contingency decision taken.

options.text: Keep the current wording and brief the sponsor verbally on what it really means.
options.rationale: It creates two versions of the truth, one spoken and one written, and the written one is what survives, gets forwarded and is read at the inquiry.

options.text: Move the detail into an annex marked commercially sensitive.
options.rationale: It mislabels a schedule problem as commercial in order to keep it out of view, and information parked in an annex nobody opens has not been communicated.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to confirm in writing that he understood last month's report.
options.rationale: It audits the reader instead of repairing the wording that misled him, and it spends the conversation on blame rather than on the contingency you still need.

questions.explanation: A report exists so a particular person can take a particular decision, and wording chosen to survive a hypothetical hostile reader routinely fails the intended one. Where a report may be disclosed, the protection is precision — a defensible account of what happened, why, and what is being asked for — rather than language soft enough to mean nothing. Ambiguity does not reduce exposure; it just moves the reckoning to the point where the decision was never taken.
questions.mindset: Write for the decision you need, and let accuracy rather than vagueness be the defence.

questions.stem: Your squad builds appointment and notes software for a chain of physiotherapy clinics. Attendance at the fortnightly review has fallen from twelve to three over five months, and the three who still come are the clinic managers who requested the current feature. Feedback from everyone else now arrives weeks later as support tickets, two of which have caused rework. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask several of the people who stopped coming what they used to get from it and what they need instead.
options.rationale: It treats the absence as information about the session rather than about the people, and the answer determines whether the fix is content, timing or format.

options.text: Restructure the review to open with the decisions the team needs from the room, and keep it to those.
options.rationale: Attendance follows consequence. A session where an attendee's presence changes an outcome is worth the diary slot in a way that a progress walkthrough is not.

options.text: Make attendance a condition of having a feature prioritised.
options.rationale: Coerced presence produces bodies without attention, and it converts a relationship you need for candid feedback into a transaction people will game.

options.text: Record the review and circulate it to everyone who has stopped attending.
options.rationale: It turns a two-way session into a broadcast, which is precisely the direction the missing feedback needs to travel in, and recordings of meetings people skipped go unwatched.

options.text: Accept the three who attend as the real audience and stop inviting the rest.
options.rationale: It mistakes non-attendance for disinterest and locks in the narrow feedback loop that has already produced two pieces of rework.

questions.explanation: Declining attendance at a feedback session is itself feedback, and the useful response is to find out what the session stopped being worth rather than to compel or replace the audience. A review earns its place when the people in it leave having changed something, so the design question is what decisions the room is being asked for. Where the loop closes only through support tickets, the cost shows up later as rework rather than as an empty diary.
questions.mindset: Treat an empty chair as feedback about the meeting, not about the person.

questions.stem: You are three weeks from the shutdown weekend on a paper mill's boiler replacement outage, and three unrelated communication needs have landed on the same morning. Each has already gone wrong once because it was handled by whatever method was nearest to hand: a document sent to a group address, a decision attempted over email, and evidence supplied one request at a time. Match each situation to the communication method that fits what it actually has to achieve. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Twenty-six contractors' supervisors need the revised isolation procedure before Monday's shift, and each must be able to show they hold it.
Two engineering leads disagree about which of two designs to build, and each has already circulated a paper arguing their case.
The client's assurance team wants to inspect test evidence at times of their own choosing, without asking you for it each time.

options.text: A controlled document issued to a named distribution list with receipt recorded
options.rationale: Where the obligation is that specific people hold a specific version, the method has to be directed and evidenced. Receipt recording is the part that makes it auditable.

options.text: A facilitated session with both leads and the decision maker in the room
options.rationale: Two papers have already failed to resolve it, which is the signal that the remaining work is negotiation. Interactive methods are the only ones that converge a disagreement.

options.text: A shared evidence repository with access granted and an index maintained
options.rationale: Where the audience wants information on their own schedule, pull removes you from the loop entirely and stops assurance requests arriving as interruptions.

options.text: An item in the monthly all-staff bulletin
options.rationale: Not used. A general bulletin reaches everyone and commits no one. It cannot prove receipt, cannot resolve a disagreement and cannot be interrogated on demand, which is all three requirements here.

questions.explanation: Method follows what the communication has to achieve rather than what is quickest to send: proof that named people hold something, convergence between people who disagree, or availability to an audience that will come and look. Push, interactive and pull are not a hierarchy, and a project using only one of them will fail whichever need it does not serve. The tell is in the verb of the requirement — hold, agree, inspect — not in the size of the audience.
questions.mindset: Pick the method from what the communication has to achieve, not from what is quickest to send.

questions.stem: Your programme is upgrading the antenna control software at a satellite ground station. In a readiness meeting the client's operations team quotes a cutover window you moved four months ago. The current plan goes to a distribution list assembled at kick-off, and the operations team joined the project afterwards and is not on it. Three other groups have joined since. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Publish one authoritative copy of the current plan, point every audience at it, and confirm what each group is presently working from.
options.rationale: It removes the mechanism that produced the fault rather than the instance, and confirming what people hold finds the other groups before the next readiness meeting does.

options.text: Email the current plan to the operations team and apologise for the omission.
options.rationale: It repairs the one case you happened to discover, leaves the three other groups in the same position, and sends a copy that starts ageing immediately.

options.text: Rebuild the distribution list from the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: The register records who exists, not who needs which artefact. A longer list still pushes a version that will be superseded next month.

options.text: Ask each group to confirm which version they hold before every meeting.
options.rationale: It transfers version control to the audience and makes a fixable distribution fault into a standing ritual that will lapse within two months.

questions.explanation: For anything that changes, one published copy that everyone reads beats many distributed copies that diverge, because a sent document has no way of telling its reader it has been superseded. The distribution question then becomes who has been pointed at the source rather than who received which email, which is a much smaller thing to keep correct as an audience grows. When a stakeholder quotes something stale, the fault to chase is the mechanism, not the message.
questions.mindset: Make one copy authoritative, because every copy you distribute starts going out of date the moment it is sent.

questions.stem: A payroll bureau's squad moved to written-first working after two engineers said meetings were destroying their days. Proposals go into a document and are agreed in comments, and it has worked well for design choices. Last week a disagreement about whether to delay a release ran to sixty-one comments across four days, ended without resolution, and the release slipped by default. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep written-first for proposals and name the kinds of question that go straight to a live conversation.
options.rationale: It preserves a practice that is working for most decisions and carves out the class it demonstrably cannot handle, which is disagreement between people.

options.text: Reinstate a daily decision meeting so that nothing stalls in comments.
options.rationale: It discards a working practice because of the minority of cases it does not suit, and hands back the fragmented days the team changed things to escape.

options.text: Set a rule that comment threads close after twenty-four hours, with the author deciding.
options.rationale: It puts a deadline on a medium that was never going to converge the disagreement, producing a decision the participants have not accepted and will relitigate.

options.text: Ask the product owner to rule whenever a thread passes twenty comments.
options.rationale: It uses thread length as the trigger rather than the nature of the question, and escalates a judgement the same people still have to accept afterwards.

questions.explanation: Asynchronous writing is strong for proposing, reviewing and recording, and weak for negotiating, because a disagreement needs the participants to hear each other adjust in real time. The useful team agreement is not a rule about volume but a rule about kind: proposals in writing, conflicts in a room. A default that decides by exhaustion is still a decision, and it is the one nobody would have chosen.
questions.mindset: Match the medium to whether the work is proposing or negotiating.

questions.stem: Your project installs a new compressor house at a tyre remoulding plant, which needs eleven weeks of the staff car park. The plan was to announce it next Monday alongside the shuttle bus arrangements, once that contract is signed. On Wednesday a survey crew arrived and marked out the bays. By Thursday the works committee believed parking was being removed permanently and had requested a meeting. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Announce today what is decided, what is not yet decided, and when the rest will be known.
options.rationale: It takes back the timing from the paint on the tarmac, and separating settled facts from open ones is what stops a partial announcement being read as a full one.

options.text: Hold to Monday and ask supervisors to tell their teams that nothing has been decided.
options.rationale: It asks people to deny something the workforce can see, and it spends the supervisors' credibility on a message that will be contradicted within days.

options.text: Instruct the surveyors not to discuss their work with plant staff.
options.rationale: It chases the leak rather than the vacuum, and there is no version of marked-out bays in a shared car park that stays invisible for five days.

options.text: Wait for Monday and address the rumours as part of the announcement.
options.rationale: It concedes four more days for an unmanaged story to harden, after which the announcement lands as a reaction to the rumour rather than as news.

questions.explanation: Where a change is physically visible, the timetable for telling people is set by what they can see rather than by when the last arrangement is signed. Waiting for a complete message reliably produces an incomplete one from somewhere else, and correcting a settled belief costs far more than forming it first. Announcing with the open questions named — and a date for answering them — is almost always better than announcing later with everything resolved.
questions.mindset: Announce before the evidence does, because a rumour is a vacuum filling itself.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is replacing a university's student records system, with a predictive integration workstream alongside an incrementally delivered front end. An internal audit has criticised the programme on two counts: decisions that cannot be traced afterwards, and reporting that leaves stakeholders no way of checking anything for themselves. Two situations from this week are instances of each criticism. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A decision to drop two reports from the first release was reached in a chat thread between the product owner and two analysts, and nobody outside the thread knows. The decision should be
The finance director asks for direct read access to the delivery team's raw defect data rather than the summary in your monthly report. The request should be

options.text: recorded in the decision log with its date, its owner and its reason, then noted in the next report
options.rationale: The reason is the part that becomes unrecoverable, and the people who will ask why the reports are missing are not the people who were in the thread.

options.text: granted as a view she can read whenever she likes, with the summary still going into the report
options.rationale: A stakeholder who wants the underlying data is asking for access rather than for more sending, and refusing it makes the curated summary look like management of her.

options.text: left as it stands, since everyone who needed to agree it was already in the conversation
options.rationale: Not used. Agreement is not the same as record. The people who needed to agree are a smaller group than the people who will later need to know why, and the thread will be unfindable long before the question is asked.

questions.explanation: Transparency is about what a stakeholder can reach rather than about how much you send them, and the two situations show its opposite failures: a decision that exists only in a private conversation, and information withheld behind a summary that nobody asked to be the only route. Recording decisions where they can be found, and granting access where somebody wants to look, both cost less than the alternative and both reduce what you have to broadcast.
questions.mindset: Transparency is access to what exists, not more of what you send.

questions.stem: Your squad builds the flight planning tool for a drone survey business. The sponsor meets a launch customer on Friday and asks when the mapping export will be ready. Four sprints of throughput put it between mid-March and late April, depending on how much of the coordinate conversion turns out to be reusable — something the team will know within three weeks. He says a range is no use to him. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Give the range with what drives each end, name the one thing that will narrow it and when, and ask what he needs the date for.
options.rationale: It gives him something usable on Friday while keeping the uncertainty attached, and the question about purpose often changes which commitment he actually needs.

options.text: Give late April, since it is the safe end of the range.
options.rationale: It buys safety by knowingly overstating, and when the work lands in March the forecast is disbelieved in the other direction next time.

options.text: Give mid-March and manage the risk as the sprints run.
options.rationale: It commits someone else to your optimism in front of a customer, and the cost of being wrong lands on the person who repeated the date rather than on you.

options.text: Decline to give a date until the coordinate conversion is understood.
options.rationale: It leaves the sponsor to invent a figure in the meeting, which is the least informed forecast available and the one you will be held to anyway.

questions.explanation: Removing the uncertainty from a forecast does not remove it from the project; it just moves it to whoever repeats the number. What makes a range usable is the account of what drives each end and what will resolve it, which turns an unsatisfying answer into a plan for a better one. Asking what the date is for is not evasion — a date for a contract, a marketing calendar and an internal expectation carry very different consequences for being wrong.
questions.mindset: Give the uncertainty with the number, because someone will act on the number either way.

questions.stem: Fourteen months into a two-year customs declaration system for a port authority, your sponsor moves to another division. Her replacement arrives from operations, has never sponsored a project, and opens your first meeting by asking for everything you have got. The document set runs to about four hundred pages. The next funding release is decided in five weeks. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Brief him against the decisions he will have to take this quarter, beginning with the funding release.
options.rationale: A new decision maker needs the decisions before the history, because the history only becomes navigable once he knows what he is being asked to settle.

options.text: Walk him through the commitments the project has already made that he now owns, and where each was agreed.
options.rationale: Inherited commitments are the part a new sponsor is most likely to contradict unknowingly, and knowing where each was agreed is what lets him defend or change them deliberately.

options.text: Send the full document set so he can decide for himself what he needs.
options.rationale: It outsources filtering to the person least equipped to do it, and four hundred pages five weeks before a funding decision guarantees none of it is read.

options.text: Let him settle in and keep reporting as you have been.
options.rationale: It assumes a report is self-explanatory to a reader with no history of the project, and spends the five weeks before a funding decision on that assumption.

options.text: Give him a one-page status summary and offer to answer any questions.
options.rationale: It answers how the project is going, when his actual gap is not knowing what he is accountable for, and it makes him name questions he does not yet know exist.

questions.explanation: Briefing a new decision maker is organised around the decisions rather than around the archive, because volume is what a newcomer has least capacity to process and least ability to filter. The commitments already made in their name are the highest-value content, since those are what they will otherwise contradict in public. Handing someone the document set is the appearance of transparency without any of its function.
questions.mindset: Brief a new sponsor on what they must decide, not on what has happened.

questions.stem: Your team builds a mooring permit product for a canal trust. The head of the volunteer wardens came to the first two reviews, has missed the last six, and has told two trustees that the product will be unusable on the towpath. He has raised nothing with you directly. A trustee forwards you his message and asks you to sort out the negativity. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Go to him, on the towpath if that is where he works, and find out what he has seen that you have not.
options.rationale: He is the closest thing you have to a user test, and the objection is specific enough to be either a real defect or a fixable misunderstanding — you cannot tell which from here.

options.text: Ask the trustees to hear his concern formally so it can be answered on the record.
options.rationale: It escalates an objection into a contest before you know what it is, and gives it a larger and more permanent platform than a conversation would have.

options.text: Demonstrate the towpath workflow at the next review and make sure he is invited.
options.rationale: It answers an objection you have guessed at, in a forum he has already stopped attending, which is two assumptions stacked on each other.

options.text: Record him in the register as a resistant stakeholder and work around him.
options.rationale: It labels the person instead of learning from them, and the wardens are the users whose adoption decides whether any of this works.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder who has stopped talking to you is still communicating, and treating withdrawal as an attitude problem forfeits the information in it. The first move is to re-establish a direct channel on their ground and listen for the specific thing behind the general complaint, because criticism routed to third parties usually means the direct route felt unavailable. Resistance framed as a personality is rarely actionable; resistance traced to a concrete observation nearly always is.
questions.mindset: Go and find out what someone knows before deciding they are being difficult.

questions.stem: The timeline shows one reporting cycle on a hospital pharmacy automation project. Site data is collected on Tuesday, your report is written on Wednesday and issued on Thursday, the programme office consolidates on the following Monday, and the board meets the Tuesday after that. A director has complained that the board decides on stale figures. Select the interval that sets how old the oldest figure in the board pack can be.

graphic.title: One reporting cycle from site data collection to the board meeting
graphic.caption: Select an interval. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Site collection through to the board meeting
regions.rationale: A figure ages from the moment it is captured to the moment it is used to decide, so every leg in between counts. Naming the whole span is what makes the eight-day lag visible as a design choice rather than an accident.

regions.label: Site collection to your report being issued
regions.rationale: This is your own turnaround and the shortest leg on the chart. Teams under pressure optimise here, gain two days at most, and stay puzzled that the board still sees old numbers.

regions.label: Your report issued to programme office consolidation
regions.rationale: A single middle leg. It contributes to the total but naming it alone understates the age of the data by the collection and board legs on either side.

regions.label: Programme office consolidation to the board meeting
regions.rationale: The last leg only, and the one most visible to the board, which is why it attracts the blame. The figures were already several days old before consolidation started.

questions.explanation: Information ages from capture rather than from publication, so the latency that matters is the whole chain from measurement to decision. Attacking one leg because it is the one you control produces a marginal gain and leaves the complaint intact; the useful move is to publish the total lag, let the governance body see what it is buying with each handoff, and let them decide which leg to shorten. A status figure without its as-at date is an invitation to this argument.
questions.mindset: Measure the age of a figure from when it was taken, not from when you sent it.

questions.stem: Your squad shares a chat channel with staff at the bicycle parts distributor you are building a stock allocation tool for. It was opened to speed up questions and it has. On Tuesday a developer wrote that the overnight reconciliation was probably double counting returns. It was a hunch, and it was wrong. By Wednesday the client's finance director had halted the returns write-off run and asked for an explanation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the channel and agree with the client what it is for, including how the team signals that something is unverified.
options.rationale: The failure is a missing shared convention, not a missing person. Agreeing how speculation is marked keeps the speed everyone gained and removes the ambiguity that caused the shutdown.

options.text: Close the channel and route all client questions through you.
options.rationale: It removes the speed the channel was created for, and makes you a bottleneck that both sides will work around within a fortnight.

options.text: Ask the developer to be more careful about what he writes in front of the client.
options.rationale: It puts a shared design fault on one person, and leaves the next engineer's next hunch to be governed by their own private judgement.

options.text: Post a correction and ask the finance director to check with you before acting on anything in the channel.
options.rationale: It asks the client to distrust a channel you are still inviting them to use, which is an unstable arrangement that will end with them leaving it.

questions.explanation: A channel shared with a client carries two audiences reading by different conventions: internally, thinking aloud is how work gets done, while externally the same sentence is a statement from the supplier. The fix is an explicit agreement about what the channel is for and how tentative things are marked, because the alternative — everyone self-censoring — quietly destroys the value that made the channel worth opening. Conventions have to be stated before speed makes the channel the default.
questions.mindset: Agree what a shared channel is for before speed makes it the default.

questions.stem: A pension administration platform migration is being handed over to an incoming project manager, who says she cannot establish why any of the significant choices were made. Everything from the last eight months has gone into one long meeting narrative, so live commitments, settled decisions and background argument are interleaved and nothing can be searched. Match each thing that must be findable later to the record that should hold it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The reason the scheme actuary accepted a two-week gap in the indexation data, agreed on a call last March.
Who is doing what before Friday, settled at yesterday's coordination meeting.
What was argued, and by whom, when the trustees debated the transfer approach across two sessions.

options.text: The decision log
options.rationale: A decision log holds what was decided, by whom and why. The reason is the part that becomes unrecoverable a year later, when the decision looks strange and the people have moved on.

options.text: The action list
options.rationale: Actions are short-lived, individually owned and actively chased. Keeping them separate is what stops a live list being buried inside a record nobody reopens.

options.text: The meeting minutes
options.rationale: Minutes carry the deliberation — what was argued and how the group arrived somewhere. That is what a later reader needs when asking whether the trustees considered a point at all.

options.text: The issue register
options.rationale: Not used. An issue register tracks things that are wrong and need resolving by somebody. None of these three is an issue, and treating every record as one is how registers become a dumping ground nobody trusts.

questions.explanation: Records are separated by the question a future reader will arrive with: why was this allowed, who owes me something this week, and did anyone consider that. Collapsing them into one long narrative makes each question expensive to answer and guarantees the live items are lost among the historical ones. Deciding which record holds what is a small piece of design that decides whether the project is auditable a year after everyone has left.
questions.mindset: Separate records by the question a future reader will arrive with.

questions.stem: A squad building a route planning app for a rural bus operator currently sends the same fortnightly summary to three very different audiences, and none of them has ever acted on it. The squad's instinct is to make the summary better. Before rewriting anything, work out what each audience is actually deciding and how often. Match each audience to the update that fits how it decides. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The six drivers piloting the app, who need to know what changes in tomorrow's build.
The operations director, who releases the next tranche of funding at a monthly meeting.
The transport authority's contract manager, who checks quarterly that agreed outcomes are being met.

options.text: A short note in the depot messaging group each evening, listing what changed
options.rationale: Drivers make one decision — how to work tomorrow — so the update has to arrive before the shift, in the place they already look, and contain only what changed.

options.text: A one-page monthly summary of value delivered, spend, and the decision being asked for
options.rationale: A funding decision needs the case in front of it at the moment it is taken. Anything arriving between meetings is read as noise because nothing can be done with it.

options.text: A quarterly report mapping delivered functionality to the outcomes in the agreement
options.rationale: A contractual audience is checking conformance rather than progress, so the report has to be organised by their obligations rather than by your delivery order.

options.text: A live burndown chart shared with all three audiences
options.rationale: Not used. A burndown answers a question the squad has about its own sprint. None of these three is trying to work out whether the sprint will finish, and sharing it invites them to manage the team's internals.

questions.explanation: Cadence and content follow the audience's decision rhythm, not the team's delivery rhythm, which is why one update reused across every audience serves none of them well. The design questions are what this audience decides, how often they decide it, and what they need in hand at that moment. An artefact built for the team's own control loop is almost always the wrong thing to hand to somebody outside it.
questions.mindset: Report on the audience's decision cycle, not on your delivery cycle.

questions.stem: You began recording the fortnightly risk workshop on a credit union's core banking replacement so that two members who cannot attend can catch up. Across three sessions the workshop has grown shorter, and the operations manager, who used to raise most of the uncomfortable items, now sends you her concerns privately afterwards. The recordings are watched by nobody. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Stop recording, and meet the two absent members' need another way.
options.rationale: The recording is costing the session's whole purpose and buying something nobody uses. Removing it restores the candour, and the catch-up need is easily met by a written summary.

options.text: Keep recording and reassure the group that nothing said will be held against them.
options.rationale: A reassurance cannot undo the existence of a permanent record. People calibrate to who might eventually listen, not to the assurance of whoever is in the room.

options.text: Keep recording but restrict access to the two absentees.
options.rationale: The constraint on candour is that the record exists at all, not who currently has the link, and access rules change more easily than recordings disappear.

options.text: Ask the operations manager to raise her items in the session as she used to.
options.rationale: It asks one person to absorb a cost the format created, and ignores that the rest of the group has silently made the same calculation.

questions.explanation: The method changes the content: a channel that creates a durable record will always reduce what people are willing to put into it, and a risk session depends entirely on what people are willing to say. Where a convenience for absent members conflicts with the purpose of the session for those present, the purpose wins and the convenience is met some other way. Falling duration and privately routed concerns are the two clearest signals that a format has started suppressing its own input.
questions.mindset: Ask what a channel does to what people are willing to say, not only to who receives it.

questions.stem: Your parent company is in a takeover offer period, and its legal counsel has instructed all project managers that nothing about capital projects may be said externally until the offer closes, which could be six weeks or ten. Your biscuit line automation project reaches its first production run in three weeks. Forty line operators, two supplier engineers and the site's union representative are all expecting a briefing. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish with counsel exactly what the restriction covers, then brief the internal audiences on operational matters and say plainly what cannot be discussed and why.
options.rationale: Restrictions have edges, and the widest reading is rarely the correct one. Establishing the boundary first is what lets the operational briefing go ahead at all.

options.text: Postpone every briefing until the restriction lifts.
options.rationale: It reads a limit on external statements as a ban on running the project, and starts a production run with forty operators who have not been told how it works.

options.text: Brief the operators verbally and put nothing in writing.
options.rationale: It mistakes the medium for the restriction. A statement to forty people is a public statement whatever form it takes, and you have destroyed the record as well.

options.text: Ask your sponsor to seek an exemption so the planned briefing can go ahead.
options.rationale: It spends the sponsor's time and standing seeking permission for something almost certainly already permitted, while the three weeks to the production run run down.

questions.explanation: A communication restriction has a scope, and the first task is to find its edge rather than to assume the broadest reading and stop. Most such instructions concern external statements and leave internal operational communication untouched, so treating them as total silence creates a safety and delivery problem in order to solve a legal one that did not exist. Where something genuinely cannot be said, naming the boundary is itself informative and keeps the silence from being read as concealment.
questions.mindset: Find the edge of a restriction before letting it decide what you say.

questions.stem: A public aquarium's ticketing and membership replacement issues a weekly bulletin to 240 staff. The platform reports that 96 of them opened last week's edition. A five-question survey sent to those 96 found that 24 could correctly state the go-live weekend. Your sponsor asks whether the bulletin is working, and you want the figures in front of you before answering.

blanks.label: Percentage of recipients who opened the bulletin, to the nearest whole number
blanks.rationale: 96 of 240 is 40%. An open rate measures only that a message was retrieved, which is the weakest of the three things you might want to know.

blanks.label: Percentage of all 240 recipients demonstrated to know the go-live weekend
blanks.rationale: 24 of 240 is 10%. Comprehension has to be measured against the whole audience, not against the subset that opened, or the bulletin looks four times better than it is.

blanks.label: Number of recipients about whom the survey tells you nothing at all
blanks.rationale: 240 minus the 96 who opened leaves 144 never surveyed, and they are the group least likely to know. Sampling only the engaged flatters every figure derived from it.

questions.explanation: Delivery, retrieval and understanding are three different measurements, and only the last one is what a communication was for. Platform statistics report the sender's end of the exchange, so a project that manages by open rate is optimising the wrong quantity and will keep being surprised by what the audience does not know. Where a sample is drawn only from people who already engaged, the result is an upper bound rather than an estimate.
questions.mindset: Measure whether a message was understood, because delivery statistics measure only your end of it.

questions.stem: Your squad sends a release note to 130 people at a self-storage operator each time it ships. Because it goes from a group address, replies reach everyone. A question about pricing on Tuesday produced thirty-four replies, most of them people asking to be taken off the list. Two area managers whose sign-off you need have now filtered the address into a folder they do not open. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send the note from an address that does not accept replies, and give a named route for questions.
options.rationale: It separates the broadcast from the conversation mechanically, so the fix does not depend on 130 people remembering a convention every time they hit reply.

options.text: Ask recipients to reply only to the sender rather than to everyone.
options.rationale: It relies on a hundred and thirty people overriding the obvious button under time pressure, which fails on the first release where something is contentious.

options.text: Cut the list to the twenty people who have replied in the last six months.
options.rationale: It uses replying as a proxy for needing to know, which drops exactly the quiet majority who read the note and act on it without comment.

options.text: Move release notes into the squad's chat tool and invite everyone in.
options.rationale: It answers a reply-all problem by moving the audience to a tool they have not adopted, where the same threads form with less visibility.

questions.explanation: Broadcasting and conversing need different mechanics, and a channel that quietly permits both will produce noise that trains the audience to stop reading. The remedy is structural — a one-way route out and a named route back — because conventions that depend on every recipient behaving well fail at the worst moment. Once senior recipients have started filtering a channel, the cost is no longer noise but the sign-offs that will not arrive.
questions.mindset: Separate broadcasting from conversation, or the broadcast will teach people to stop reading.

questions.stem: On a rolling stock refurbishment, the client, the depot operator and your team work to a correspondence route agreed at contract award, under which instructions pass between named people only. The route has held for nine months. This week two things happen in quick succession that test how firmly it should be enforced and against whom. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: One of your engineers, worried about a bogie tolerance, emails the client's engineering director directly. Your immediate response should be to
The client's engineering director replies to that email agreeing a change to the tolerance. That change should be

options.text: thank him for raising it, then agree with him how a safety concern travels fast without leaving the route
options.rationale: The instinct is right and the route is wrong, and only one of those is worth correcting. Making the correction feel expensive is how a project trains people not to raise things.

options.text: treated as unconfirmed until it is issued through the agreed route, and chased there the same day
options.rationale: An agreement reached off-route binds nobody and is not traceable. Chasing it the same day keeps the technical benefit while putting the commitment where it can be relied on.

options.text: reported to the client as a breach of the correspondence protocol
options.rationale: Not used. Making the breach the headline turns an engineer's good instinct into an incident, and teaches a team that raising a concern outside the hierarchy costs more than staying quiet.

questions.explanation: A correspondence route exists so that commitments are traceable and issued by people with the authority to make them; it is not there to stop engineers talking to engineers. That distinction lets you hold the route firmly for anything that binds while keeping the path for concerns as wide as possible. Enforcing the route by penalising the person who used the wrong one buys compliance at the price of the next warning nobody gives you.
questions.mindset: Protect the route for commitments and keep the path for concerns wide open.

questions.stem: You take over a programme rolling out clinical software to a group of dental practices. The communications plan was written twenty-two months ago and specifies a monthly newsletter, a quarterly forum and a sponsor briefing. Since then the group has acquired eleven practices, the sponsor has changed, and the forum has not met for a year. The newsletter still goes out. Which two actions should the project manager take first?

options.text: Rebuild the plan from who now has to decide or do something, and what each of them needs in order to do it.
options.rationale: A communications plan is derived from the stakeholders and their decisions, so when those change the plan is stale regardless of how well it is being executed.

options.text: Find out which existing channels people actually use, by asking a sample of the audience rather than by counting what was sent.
options.rationale: Send statistics measure your own activity. Asking a handful of recipients is the cheapest way to learn which of the three channels was ever worth anything.

options.text: Restart the quarterly forum, since it is the only two-way channel in the plan.
options.rationale: It revives a channel because a document lists it, before establishing whether anyone valued it or why it lapsed in the first place.

options.text: Update the distribution lists to include the eleven new practices.
options.rationale: It extends a plan whose fitness has not been tested, so eleven more audiences begin receiving something nobody has shown to be useful.

options.text: Archive the plan and run communications directly from the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: The register records who exists, not what any of them needs. Working without a plan is how the cadence quietly disappeared the first time.

questions.explanation: A communications plan is downstream of stakeholder analysis, so any material change in who the stakeholders are or what they decide invalidates it, however faithfully the cadence has been kept. Inheriting one is an occasion to test it against the current audience rather than to resume executing it, and the test is what people use rather than what was sent. Keeping a channel because it is written down is how a plan becomes a description of a project that no longer exists.
questions.mindset: Rebuild a communications plan from the audience's decisions whenever the audience changes.

questions.stem: Your squad's mobile ticketing app for a city bus operator releases fortnightly. Under the contract, every message to passengers goes out through the operator's own communications team. Your notice about the fare capping change, which alters what passengers see at the gate, has been with them for eleven working days. The release is in four. Two emails have gone unanswered. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Telephone the communications lead today, agree a date they can actually meet, and hold the release to that date rather than the other way round.
options.rationale: It converts an unanswered queue into a commitment you can plan against, and accepts that a channel owned by someone else sets the pace of what depends on it.

options.text: Publish the notice yourself through the app's in-product messaging.
options.rationale: It bypasses a contractual route to protect your own date, and buys one release at the cost of the relationship you need at every release after it.

options.text: Escalate to your sponsor to have the contractual messaging route changed.
options.rationale: It seeks a contract variation to solve an eleven-day queue, which will take far longer than the queue and answers a question nobody has yet asked.

options.text: Release on schedule and let the operator communicate whenever they are ready.
options.rationale: It changes what passengers see without telling them, and the gap between the change and the notice is exactly where the complaints are generated.

questions.explanation: Where another organisation owns the channel to your end users, their lead time is a dependency on your plan and belongs in it with a date and an owner, not treated as a formality that will resolve itself. Escalating or bypassing both attack the arrangement rather than the queue, while a direct conversation usually produces a workable date within the hour. A release whose user-facing notice is not ready is not ready.
questions.mindset: Treat someone else's channel as a dependency with a lead time, not as a formality.

questions.stem: Two squads at a car park operator ship to the same customer app. On Thursday the payments squad emailed forty thousand registered drivers that contactless exit would go live on Monday. The enforcement squad's in-app banner, live since Tuesday, says the barrier change is postponed. The contact centre took three hundred calls on Friday morning and is asking which is true. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish the single true position with both squads and give the contact centre one answer today.
options.rationale: The people currently absorbing the contradiction cannot wait for a governance fix, and every hour without an agreed line multiplies the versions in circulation.

options.text: Agree that customer-facing messages from either squad go out only through one owner of the customer channel.
options.rationale: Two teams with independent access to the same audience will collide again on a different Thursday. Single ownership of the channel is the structural repair.

options.text: Retract the email and reissue it after Monday.
options.rationale: It leaves the contradicting banner untouched and adds a third message to an audience already holding two, which reads as an organisation that does not know what it is doing.

options.text: Instruct the enforcement squad to take the banner down.
options.rationale: It picks a message by which is easiest to withdraw rather than by which is correct, and forty thousand people have already received the other one.

options.text: Add a note to the app explaining that different teams release independently.
options.rationale: It explains your internal structure to customers, which is never an answer to the question of what is happening on Monday and reads as an excuse.

questions.explanation: A customer experiences one organisation, so the number of teams behind a channel is invisible to them and irrelevant to what they are owed. Where several teams can reach the same audience, contradiction is a matter of time, and the fix is ownership of the channel rather than better intentions in each team. The immediate obligation runs to whoever is currently absorbing the confusion, and that is usually the contact centre rather than the customer.
questions.mindset: One audience should have one owner of what it is told.

questions.stem: Your programme replaces the shift rostering and permit-to-work system for an offshore wind operator. You are eight weeks into a confidential negotiation over the software supplier's failure to deliver two modules, termination is one option, and the commercial team has said nothing may be disclosed. At the monthly all-hands an engineer asks directly whether the supplier is being replaced, adding that the team is being asked to plan around modules that may never arrive. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Say that there is a commercial discussion you cannot describe, when you expect to be able to say more, and how the team should plan in the meantime.
options.rationale: It answers the part that is genuinely his — how to plan — while naming the boundary rather than pretending there is nothing behind it.

options.text: Say that no decision has been taken, and move on.
options.rationale: Technically true and heard as evasion, and it leaves the planning question, which you are free to answer, unanswered in front of everyone.

options.text: Tell the team the negotiation is under way and ask them to keep it confidential.
options.rationale: It transfers a confidentiality obligation to forty people who never accepted it, and the first disclosure lands on one of them rather than on you.

options.text: Say you cannot comment, and offer to speak to anyone individually afterwards.
options.rationale: It repeats the restriction forty times in private and signals that the fuller version is available to whoever asks, which is worse than a single honest boundary.

questions.explanation: Confidentiality restricts content, not responsiveness, and treating the two as the same thing is what makes a restricted situation read as concealment. Almost every awkward question of this kind contains a practical one that carries no restriction at all — usually about how people should work while the matter is open — and that is the part the asker most needs answered. Neither a technically true non-answer nor a private version for whoever asks twice is a substitute, and both cost more trust than the restriction itself ever would.
questions.mindset: Name the boundary of what you cannot say, and answer everything on your side of it.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the agreed correspondence routes on a metro station accessibility upgrade. Instructions pass only between the client's project manager and yours; a direct line between the two design leads is permitted for technical queries; and your project manager directs your site agent internally. The client's cost manager has just emailed your site agent instructing a change to the lift shaft finish. Select the link that email has travelled on.

graphic.title: Agreed correspondence routes between client and contractor, with one unauthorised link
graphic.caption: Select a link. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between links, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Client project manager to your project manager — instructions
regions.rationale: This is the permitted route for instructions and the one that has been bypassed. Selecting it names where the instruction should have come from rather than where it came from.

regions.label: Client design lead to your design lead — technical queries
regions.rationale: A permitted link, but for queries rather than instructions, and neither design lead is involved here. Confusing the two is how a query quietly becomes an instruction.

regions.label: Client cost manager to your site agent
regions.rationale: This is the link the email actually used, and it appears nowhere in the agreed routes. An instruction from someone with no authority to give it, to someone with no authority to accept it, is the highest-risk correspondence a project receives.

regions.label: Your project manager to your site agent — internal direction
regions.rationale: This is how the instruction should have reached the site agent once received and accepted. It is the step that was skipped, not the one that was used.

questions.explanation: Correspondence routes define both who may instruct and who may accept, and an instruction arriving off-route is not an instruction however senior the sender sounds. Reading the route before reading the content is what stops a site team acting on something that will later be disowned, and it is the difference between a change and an unpriced variation nobody agreed. The point of the route is that both organisations know which messages bind them.
questions.mindset: Check who was entitled to send an instruction before deciding what to do with it.

questions.stem: The market superintendent who signs off your stall allocation product will not use email; everything happens by telephone. Yesterday he told a trader that he had never agreed to drop the paper day sheet, which you and he settled by phone six weeks ago and which the squad has already built around. He is not being dishonest, and at sixty-three he is not about to change how he works. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the telephone as his channel, and start sending a short written confirmation after every call, agreed with him as the record unless he says otherwise.
options.rationale: It works with the channel he actually uses and adds the record it lacks, putting the effort on the person who needs the decision to hold.

options.text: Ask him to confirm past decisions in writing so the record is complete.
options.rationale: It asks the one thing he does not do, about the decisions he already disputes, which will produce neither the record nor the relationship.

options.text: Ask a trader representative to sit in on future calls as a witness.
options.rationale: It adds a person in order to make a record you could write yourself, and the presence of a witness changes what he is willing to say on the call.

options.text: Rebuild the paper day sheet, since there is no evidence the decision was taken.
options.rationale: It treats an absent record as a reversed decision and spends the squad's capacity proving that anything unwritten is free to undo later.

questions.explanation: You do not get to choose other people's channels, only what you build around them, and confirming in writing after the fact works with any channel including the ones you would not have picked. The habit costs a few minutes per call and converts a disputed recollection into something the other party had the chance to correct. Demanding that a stakeholder change how they communicate is the slowest available route to a record, and it usually fails.
questions.mindset: Take people's channel as given and build the record around it.

questions.stem: A zoo's new primate enclosure is governed by a trustees' board whose next two meetings are 2 June and 1 September, with papers required ten working days beforehand, meaning 19 May and 18 August. On 20 May your contractor needs a decision on switching to a laminated glazing specification, and stops work without one. Standstill costs £3,400 a day. Work out the wait before deciding what to propose.

blanks.label: Days from 20 May to the first board meeting that could take the decision
blanks.rationale: The 2 June papers deadline passed on 19 May, so the next available meeting is 1 September: 11 days of May, 30 of June, 31 of July, 31 of August and 1 of September, giving 104.

blanks.label: Cost of standstill across that wait, in £
blanks.rationale: 104 days at £3,400 is £353,600. Putting the number on the delay is what turns a governance inconvenience into a decision the board can weigh.

blanks.label: The governance mechanism that would let a decision of this kind be taken between meetings
blanks.rationale: Delegated authority — a named person able to decide up to a defined threshold between meetings — is what removes latency without adding meetings, and it has to be agreed before it is needed.

questions.explanation: Reporting exists so decisions can be taken, so the cadence that matters is the decision cycle rather than the reporting cycle, and a project whose governance meets quarterly has a quarterly decision latency however often it reports. The remedy is a delegated route agreed in advance with a threshold and a named holder, because arguing for one during a standstill costs the standstill. Quantifying the delay is what makes the case, since a board that has never seen the cost of its own calendar has no reason to change it.
questions.mindset: Design the decision route to the speed the work needs, before the work needs it.

questions.stem: Your programme piloted a triage tool in three of a hearing aid group's forty clinics. Over eight weeks and 340 appointments, average waiting time in those three fell from 26 days to 19. Your sponsor's slide to the group board reads: new triage cuts waits by 27 per cent. The board has asked for a national rollout date. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Give the sponsor the same figure with its scope and confidence attached, in a form he can actually put on a slide.
options.rationale: A caveat that will not fit the medium does not travel, so the useful help is a short, quotable version that carries its own conditions.

options.text: Tell him plainly, before a rollout date is agreed, what the pilot does and does not support.
options.rationale: The rollout decision is about to be made on the overstated figure, and the only person who knows the scope is you. Saying so before the date is set is the whole window.

options.text: Correct the record directly with the board secretariat.
options.rationale: It goes around the sponsor to fix his slide, which costs the relationship that gets your figures in front of the board at all next time.

options.text: Accept the figure, since it is arithmetically correct for the three clinics.
options.rationale: A true number in the wrong scope is a false claim, and correctness in the source data is not a defence once it has been generalised to forty sites.

options.text: Ask for a larger pilot before any rollout date is agreed.
options.rationale: It answers a communication failure with more evidence, when the evidence you have has simply been described wrongly and the description is what needs fixing.

questions.explanation: A figure travels without its conditions unless the conditions are packaged to travel with it, so handing over a number and a footnote reliably produces the number alone. Scope, sample and duration are part of the finding rather than decoration on it, and the person closest to the data is the only one who can attach them.
